name: Carlos Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government, and your answers stay confidential. What is your working day usually like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to Birch Lane Accounts before the phones start because I need quiet to match the small shop receipts to bank lines. I'm 43, a junior accountant, and still slow on the tax rules; I have a bachelor's degree in accounting, but I came into the firm after years in retail. I like making a pile of crumpled receipts turn into something the owner can use, and I hate sending a question back because I missed a simple line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do money and new tools fit into the week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rosa drives a bus, and our two children, aged nine and twelve, have school bags by the door before dawn. We have a mortgage, my junior pay is low for accounting, and less than one month of bills is saved; there are few other firms nearby. I use AI every day to suggest categories for receipts and to explain a rule, then check it against the book. I believe in earning a place through work, and I try new tools quickly because waiting does not pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop owners that a quicker receipt sort is useful, but their returns still need checking. I'd probably show the junior desk one example where the tool put a bus ticket under stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet picture does not fix the thin bank balance or my slow work. The firm could still let a junior go if tax season is weak. One missed wage would put our mortgage in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for receipt categories and compare each suggestion with the bank line before signing my section. Starting this month, Rosa and I would cut takeaway meals twice a week and put forty into a mortgage buffer every payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even if AI stays small. Our household has no spare month to lose a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go first if a pay cheque were late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The broadband could wait a week, but the mortgage cannot. Rosa's bus pay covers food, not the full loan and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the buffer buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty a payday will not save the house by itself. It gives us a little less fear when a school trip form comes home.

say: I would say **receipt sorting** still needs a human check.
I would show the team a **wrong category** before trusting a result.
think: A weak season could cost my **junior wage** even without major AI change.
One missed cheque could threaten our **mortgage**.
do: Keep checking **bank lines** beside daily AI receipt suggestions.
Cut **takeaway meals** twice weekly to free cash.
Save **forty per payday** in a mortgage buffer.
feel: He feels **anxious** because one lost wage could threaten the mortgage.
S0.quote: One missed wage would put our mortgage in trouble.
fieldNote: His baseline risk is **low junior pay** against a mortgage and two children, not a new technology shock.
He already uses AI **daily** and makes small cash changes that do not pretend to solve the whole loan.

steps.text: Keep checking bank lines beside daily AI receipt suggestions
Save forty per payday in mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners that the people doing the basic returns need a fair shot at learning the harder files. I would ask what paid work remains for juniors when the software handles the first pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing letters, checking totals and answering clients fill my day, and the system could do those first. I'm still learning and not one of the top people, so I expect my hours to be cut before a senior's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to shadow the senior tax reviewer for one paid afternoon each week if the firm approves it, and use the AI error log to learn why a return fails. In the first year of steady change, if my hours are cut, I'd apply to the two local firms only when they post paid junior work and take extra evening shifts at Rosa's cousin's shop if available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because reduced hours would hit our mortgage before I have time to catch up. Learning fast is useful, but it does not replace this week's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop shifts cover the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, Rosa's cousin may need help taking stock twice a week, and the pay would be small. I would ask the rate and take those shifts only when Rosa is home with our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children that I may come home later while I learn a new part of the job. I wouldn't tell them a machine has already taken my chair when no cut has happened yet.

say: I would ask for **paid shadowing** on harder tax returns.
I would demand a **junior work plan** before first-pass tasks disappear.
think: Most of my **writing and checking** may disappear because AI takes the first pass of returns.
My **hours may fall** before a senior accountant’s do.
do: Shadow the **senior reviewer** one paid afternoon weekly if approved.
Apply for **posted junior vacancies** if my paid hours fall.
Take **available paid stock shifts** only with a confirmed rate and Rosa covering our children.
feel: He feels **alarmed** because a loss of hours could threaten mortgage payments.
S1.quote: Learning fast is useful, but it does not replace this week's pay.
fieldNote: He recognizes that his **low standing** places him first in line for lost routine hours.
Every fallback has a **paid-hours condition**; even the cousin’s shop work needs a confirmed rate.

steps.text: Shadow senior tax reviewer on paid afternoons if firm approves
Apply to posted paid junior roles if accounting hours fall
Take available paid stock shifts if rate confirmed and Rosa covers children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking work on my desk, and our family needs a real timetable from the partners. I would not call a lesson in software a job guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date hits my accounts and tax returns; the robots coming around 2031 do not delay that. I expect my junior post could disappear, and Rosa's bus driving could face robots later, leaving both wages exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the children's paid sports club for one term and add the fee to our mortgage buffer now, though I hate that choice. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I'd apply for any posted paid accounts-control job within bus distance and take confirmed evening stock shifts only on nights Rosa is home with our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and short of time. The mortgage does not wait for a clever new title on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the club fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixty a month for both children. I'd tell them we will use the public pitch for a term, and I'd restore the club only after the mortgage buffer reaches a full month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you move to a bigger job market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a written salary offer that covers the loan and a place for Rosa to work. I cannot ask the children to change schools on the chance of an interview.

say: I would demand a **real staffing timetable** before 2028.
I would tell staff **software training** is no job guarantee.
think: My **junior post** could end when AGI reaches desk work in 2028.
Rosa’s **bus work** may face robots around 2031.
do: Pause the **sixty monthly** sports club for one term.
Add **sixty monthly** to the mortgage buffer only while the sports club is paused.
Apply for **posted paid accounts-control jobs** if my post ends after 2028.
feel: He feels **alarmed** about both wages and a mortgage with little cushion.
S2.quote: The mortgage does not wait for a clever new title on my CV.
fieldNote: The sports cut is a **specific family cost**, with a condition for restoring it.
Relocation needs **written mortgage-covering pay** and work for Rosa before the children change schools.

steps.text: Pause sports club for one term; restore after one-month mortgage buffer
Add sixty monthly to mortgage buffer only while sports club is paused
Apply for posted paid accounts-control jobs if post ends after 2028
Take confirmed paid stock shifts after job loss when Rosa covers children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team five years is enough to ask for paid practice in work the firm still sells. A speech about being flexible is worth nothing if the rota loses a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031, still paying the mortgage, and AGI could do even the returns I finally learn to handle. Rosa's hands-on bus work may change when robots arrive around 2034, so we need both wages before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm for paid time on disputed shop accounts next year, and keep adding forty each payday to reach three months of mortgage payments. In the first year after 2031, if my accounting hours fall below four days a week, I'd apply for posted paid payroll-clerk jobs at the local hospital while keeping any funded firm hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me time to prove I can handle a tougher file. I still cannot pay for a long unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the disputed work look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop owner says the till says one amount and the bank shows another. I would sit with the senior reviewer on a paid shift and trace the gap with the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hospital has no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the firm hours I can get and watch posted vacancies at the other two firms. I wouldn't tell Rosa a job exists until there is an offer with a wage.

say: I would demand **paid practice** on disputed shop accounts.
I would watch the **actual rota**, not a promise of flexibility.
think: At **48 in 2031**, I still carry a mortgage and two children through school.
Rosa’s **bus income** may face robots around 2034.
do: Save **forty per payday** toward three mortgage payments.
After 2031, seek **hospital payroll** if work falls below four days; if no opening, keep firm hours and watch other firms.
feel: He feels **anxious**, with time for paid practice but little course money.
S3.quote: A speech about being flexible is worth nothing if the rota loses a day.
fieldNote: His hour threshold is **four paid days**, and the hospital application requires an actual posted job.
He wants to learn on **funded shifts** while building a modest mortgage buffer.

steps.text: Take paid disputed-account shifts if firm offers them next year
Save forty per payday toward three mortgage payments
Apply for posted paid hospital payroll jobs if hours fall below four days weekly
Keep funded firm hours; watch other two firms' postings until an offer with wages arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should be enough for the partners to give juniors a path to harder work, with pay while we learn it. I would still want them to say what happens after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives at the desk, the children may be grown, but the mortgage might not be finished. Ten years could let me pay down the loan and move out of routine returns, though robots around 2039 might also affect Rosa's bus route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a hundred a month to the mortgage principal whenever Rosa and I both have full hours, and ask the firm for a paid route into small-business payroll checks. In the first year after 2036, if the firm cuts my return hours, I'd apply for advertised salaried payroll posts and take only a written offer that covers the mortgage; if no vacancy exists, I'd keep funded hours and the buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, because ten years can help us pay down debt but does not promise a job at 53. I can see a path if both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to find the hundred?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car is old but paid off, so we'd keep it instead of taking a car loan. The hundred comes from avoiding that new monthly payment while both our shifts remain full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan retirement sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our savings are too thin today for that idea. I'd rather reduce the mortgage and stay employed as long as the firm has paid work.

say: I would ask for a **paid payroll path** inside the firm.
I would seek a clear **2036 staffing answer** for junior workers.
think: At **53 in 2036**, the mortgage may still need paying.
Rosa’s **bus route** may face robots around 2039.
do: Pay **one hundred extra monthly** off the mortgage while both work full hours.
Learn **small-business payroll checks** on paid firm time if offered.
Apply for **advertised salaried payroll posts** if return hours fall after 2036.
feel: He feels **uneasy** because debt may remain at 53.
S4.quote: I'd rather reduce the mortgage and stay employed as long as the firm has paid work.
fieldNote: He rejects early retirement and ties debt repayment to **both full-time wages**.
His 2036 fallback needs a **posted salaried role** that covers the mortgage; no vacancy means retaining funded hours.

steps.text: Pay one hundred extra monthly off mortgage while both have full hours
Learn small-business payroll checks on paid firm time if offered
Seek posted payroll job after 2036 hour cuts; accept only written mortgage-covering offer
Keep funded firm hours if no paid payroll vacancy appears after 2036 cuts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a junior accounting wage could vanish before our mortgage buffer reaches one month. Paid practice on real disputed files and a posted job with a wage would help. I cannot hand the lender a certificate and call it a payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the children give up when an adult loses one day of paid work. A missed shift is not an idea in our house; it is the sports club and next week's shopping.

headlineQuote: I cannot hand the lender a certificate and call it a payment.
portrait: Carlos, **43**, is a junior accountant at Birch Lane with an accounting bachelor’s degree after years in retail.
He earns **low pay**, has less than a month saved, a mortgage, two school-age children and few nearby accounting firms.
He uses AI **daily** for receipts but still checks bank lines, while Rosa drives a bus.
He is already **anxious** in a plateau and fears 2028 desk job loss before the household builds a buffer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior wage before the mortgage buffer reaches one month.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** on disputed files and a posted job with wages would help him meet the mortgage.
